title: Amos 4:6–13
context: The LORD recounts a series of disciplines (famine, drought, crop failure, plague, war, and overthrow like Sodom and Gomorrah), and after each comes the refrain “yet you haven’t returned to me”. The section ends with a summons to meet God and a doxology naming the Creator. Both traditions read the refrain as God’s patient warnings ignored. They differ, as they do elsewhere, on how God’s calls relate to the grace that turns a heart; see the Deuteronomy 10:16 box for that fork, and see the Judges 9:23 box on God’s hand in calamity.

verses.text: “I also have given you cleanness of teeth in all your cities, and lack of bread in every town; yet you haven’t returned to me,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD gave “cleanness of teeth”, meaning empty mouths and famine. Arminian readers see God using hardship as a call to repentance that Israel could have heeded but refused. The refrain “yet you haven’t returned to me” assumes a real possibility of turning, which grace makes possible and people can resist.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s providential discipline exposing the depth of Israel’s hardness. Hardship alone does not change a heart; turning comes as God grants it. Shared ground: the call is sincere and the refusal is culpable.

verses.text: “I also have withheld the rain from you, when there were yet three months to the harvest; and I caused it to rain on one city, and caused it not to rain on another city. One field was rained on, and the field where it didn’t rain withered.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD withholds rain at a crucial time and sends it on one city but not another. Arminian readers note that the selective rain makes the message unmistakable: these are not random events but signs meant to turn the people back to the covenant LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress God’s detailed control of weather, field by field. Shared ground: the covenant curses of drought in the Law stand behind this, and God governs creation to speak to his people.

verses.text: So two or three cities staggered to one city to drink water, and were not satisfied; yet you haven’t returned to me,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Thirsty people stagger from city to city and are not satisfied. Arminian readers hear the repeated refrain as God’s persistent pleading, each blow a renewed invitation. The failure to return is Israel’s own refusal of a sincere call.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear the same repetition as proof that discipline, by itself, does not produce repentance. Shared ground: the people’s unsatisfied thirst points beyond water to their need for the LORD, whom they have not sought.

verses.text: “I struck you with blight and mildew many times in your gardens and your vineyards, and the swarming locusts have devoured your fig trees and your olive trees; yet you haven’t returned to me,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Blight, mildew, and locusts strike gardens, vineyards, figs, and olives. Arminian readers see judgments measured to warn before final ruin, consistent with a God who wants his people to turn and live. The refrain repeats Israel’s choice not to respond.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the same losses as God’s righteous judgments, which leave the guilty without excuse. Shared ground: the loss of produce is not mere misfortune; it is the LORD speaking through his covenant warnings.

verses.text: “I sent plagues among you like I did Egypt. I have slain your young men with the sword, and have carried away your horses. I filled your nostrils with the stench of your camp, yet you haven’t returned to me,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD sent “plagues among you like I did Egypt”, reversing the exodus so that Israel experiences what Egypt suffered. Arminian readers see a sobering warning that covenant privilege does not protect a people who persist in rebellion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also see the exodus reversed and stress that God’s judgment falls on Israel when it acts like Egypt. Shared ground: war, loss of young men, and the stench of the camp are signs of the covenant curse, and still the people do not return.

verses.text: “I have overthrown some of you, as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and you were like a burning stick plucked out of the fire; yet you haven’t returned to me,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Some were overthrown “as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah,” recalling Genesis 19. Israel was rescued “like a burning stick plucked out of the fire”, an image Zechariah 3:2 also uses. Arminian readers see mercy mixed with judgment: a narrow escape that should have led to repentance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same narrow rescue as undeserved mercy that Israel failed to answer with gratitude. Shared ground: those barely saved from the fire still did not return, which exposes how deep the people’s resistance ran.

verses.text: “Therefore I will do this to you, Israel; because I will do this to you, prepare to meet your God, Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: The summons to “prepare to meet your God, Israel” comes after the refrain closes. Arminian readers often hear a final summons in which the encounter is judgment, yet a call to be ready still implies responsibility. The verse does not spell out what “this” is, and interpreters leave it open.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers usually hear the summons primarily as a threat of judgment, though later preaching has also used it as a call to repentance. Shared ground: Israel will meet God, and the encounter with the holy LORD is not something to be taken lightly.

verses.text: For, behold, he who forms the mountains, creates the wind, declares to man what is his thought, who makes the morning darkness, and treads on the high places of the earth: The LORD, the God of Armies, is his name.”
verses.arminianNotes: The doxology names the Creator who “forms the mountains” and “creates the wind”. The phrase “declares to man what is his thought” can mean God reveals his own thoughts or makes known a person’s thoughts; both readings appear. Arminian readers stress that the God who judges is the Maker of all.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the hymn grounding the threat of judgment in God’s sovereign power over all creation. “The LORD, the God of Armies, is his name” closes the section. Shared ground: the Creator who darkens the morning is the God Israel must meet.
